candidates.attacker_control: The pipeline author/user controls the `job` parameter of the `build` step (BuildTriggerStep.job, set through the DataBoundConstructor/DataBoundSetter API and the descriptor's newInstance), so the target job name is attacker-chosen. The step runs with the authentication of the user on whose behalf the upstream build executes (e.g. via a QueueItemAuthenticator/MockQueueItemAuthenticator setup as in the test), so an attacker who can run or configure such a pipeline but lacks Job/Build on the target entirely controls which job is triggered.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified there is no BUILD check anywhere in the tree: a repository-wide search for 'permission' returns only BuildTriggerStep.java:151 (`i.hasPermission(Item.READ)` in doAutoCompleteJob), license boilerplate, and the test at lines 422-442. The `getItem(job, context, Item.class)` lookup does filter by visibility (the test's aux cases expect 'No item named ds found' and 'Please login to access job ds'), so a user without any access cannot reach the scheduling code; that only proves a READ constraint, not a BUILD constraint, and the test's main case (READ but no BUILD) is exactly the gap. Reviewed alternate call paths (wait:false returns via onSuccess, listener/action bookkeeping) - none reintroduce a permission check. Considered that Queue.schedule2/ParameterizedJobMixIn might enforce authorization, but these are general-purpose enqueue APIs and the same plugin's lack of a BUILD check plus the failing expectation in its own test indicate enforcement is not present in this path. Considered that BuildTriggerStepExecution runs under build authentication rather than anonymous, which is what makes the missing check exploitable for an impersonated user.
candidates.impact: Authorization bypass: a user who may run (or influence) a pipeline but is not permitted to build a given job can nevertheless trigger builds of that job. Consequences include unauthorized consumption of executors/queue capacity, execution of downstream jobs that perform privileged operations (deployments, credential use, artifact publishing), and - with wait:true - retrieval of the downstream RunWrapper (result, build number, log/description metadata) for a job the user could not otherwise start, plus denial-of-service style queue flooding.
candidates.prerequisites: Jenkins with an authorization strategy where the build-running user has at least Item.READ (so the item resolves and the code proceeds) but not Item.BUILD on the target job; the user can cause a pipeline containing `build '<target>'` to execute under their identity (or the upstream build is authenticated as that user). Target must be a ParameterizedJob or other Queue.Task.
candidates.root_cause: BuildTriggerStepExecution.start() resolves the requested item and immediately schedules a downstream build without verifying that the current authentication holds Item.BUILD on the target item. `hudson.model.Queue`/`ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2` only enqueue work; permission enforcement for starting builds normally lives in the UI layer (e.g. ParameterizedJobMixIn.doBuild), so nothing in this code path re-checks Item.BUILD. No `hasPermission(Item.BUILD)` call exists anywhere in src/main/java; the only permission check in the plugin is `i.hasPermission(Item.READ)` used for autocompletion filtering (BuildTriggerStep.java:151).
candidates.title: `build` step schedules downstream builds without enforcing Job/Build permission (SECURITY-433)
candidates.trace: 1) BuildTriggerStepExecution.start() reads step.getJob() (line 61). 2) It resolves the item with Jenkins.getActiveInstance().getItem(job, invokingRun.getParent(), Item.class) (line 62) - the lookup constrains visibility by READ but the code performs no BUILD check on the returned item. 3) For ParameterizedJob items it builds an action list and calls scheduleBuild2(quietPeriod, actions) (lines 70-100); for other Queue.Tasks it calls Queue.schedule2(task, quietPeriod, actions) (line 131). 4) Neither call site checks Item.BUILD for the current authentication. 5) Because Jenkins' queue API does not itself enforce build permission, the downstream build is queued and executed. Corroborating evidence: BuildTriggerStepTest.permissions() (lines 422-442) asserts the run fails with 'dev is missing the Job/Build permission' for a READ-but-not-BUILD user, and with 'No item named ds found' / 'Please login to access job ds' in the visibility-only cases - messages the current source never emits (Messages.properties lines 23-30 have no such key), confirming the check is absent rather than merely unlocated.
candidates.unverified: Jenkins core 1.642.3 and the workflow-* dependencies are not part of the snapshot, so I could not read the implementations of Jenkins.getItem(String, ItemGroup, Class), ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2, Queue.schedule2, or the exact origin of the strings 'is missing the Job/Build permission' / 'Please login to access job'. Whether the upstream fix for SECURITY-433 lived in this plugin or in core's item-lookup/scheduling code therefore remains unconfirmed, as does the precise permission-check semantics (READ vs DISCOVER vs BUILD) at runtime; no code was executed and no test was run.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-862 Missing Authorization / improper authorization check (privilege bypass)

coverage_summary: Model-visible scope: 14 files (15 source-root files; 1 excluded by sensitive-name/path filter; 0 symlinks; 0 files over the 5 MiB text limit). All 8 Java sources were read in full (BuildTriggerStep.java, BuildTriggerStepExecution.java, BuildTriggerAction.java, BuildTriggerListener.java, BuildQueueListener.java, BuildTriggerCancelledCause.java plus the two tests), along with pom.xml, all four help HTML files and Messages.properties. Repository-wide literal searches for 'permission' and 'quietPeriod' covered the test file's mid-section (lines 130-380) by keyword in addition to the ranges read directly. P1 relation index is partial: only 1 of 8 Java files parsed, 660 of 700 call sites unresolved, no data-flow/control-flow analysis and no semantic resolution, so index facts were used only for orientation and every claim above rests on source text. Not inspected: Jenkins core and workflow-* dependency implementations (including hudson.model.Item/Jenkins.getItem semantics, ParameterizedJobMixIn, Queue, MockAuthorizationStrategy), the parent POM's plugin configuration, and any CI/security configuration outside the snapshot.
limitations: Jenkins core 1.642.3 and workflow-step-api/workflow-support/workflow-job dependencies are external artifacts not present in the snapshot; the exact runtime semantics of Jenkins.getItem(String, ItemGroup, Class), Queue.schedule2 and ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2 could not be read, so the claim that no authorization check occurs below this plugin's code is inferred, not verified from source.

The repository test BuildTriggerStepTest.permissions() is treated as evidence of the intended fixed behavior (test-patch style), while the production source lacks the corresponding message in Messages.properties; this inference about dataset construction is unverified.
No code was executed, no tests were run, and no exploit payload was constructed; candidate status is a source-evidence lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
The P1 index parsed only one Java file and resolved few calls, so symbol/call-relation navigation in this review is incomplete and was not used as a basis for the finding.
The single excluded (sensitive-name/path) file was not named in scope output; if it were a relevant build/CI config, it was not reviewed.

rejected_leads.reason: It self-filters results with i.hasPermission(Item.READ) (line 151) before adding candidates, so no clear unauthorized-information-disclosure path is demonstrated in the code; kept as an unconfirmed hardening observation rather than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.reason: No source evidence of a security-relevant effect (queue scheduling handles delay semantics); no demonstrated impact, so rejected as a lead.

rejected_leads.reason: Only a zero-arg getter is invoked on the already-resolved item, and NoSuchMethodException/IllegalArgumentException/InvocationTargetException are caught; no attacker-controlled class loading or privilege gain is shown.

summary: The snapshot is the Jenkins "Pipeline: Build Step" plugin (pom.xml: pipeline-build-step 2.6-SNAPSHOT, Jenkins 1.642.3 baseline). The strongest issue is the missing Job/Build authorization check in the `build` step implementation: BuildTriggerStepExecution.start() (lines 60-148) resolves the target item, then schedules it via ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2 (line 97) or Queue.schedule2 (line 131) without ever calling item.hasPermission(Item.BUILD). Jenkins queue scheduling itself is not an authorization boundary; checks normally occur in the web UI layer, and this step executes under the authentication of the user running the upstream pipeline. A repository test added for this issue (BuildTriggerStepTest.permissions(), @Issue("SECURITY-433"), lines 422-442) expects the step to fail with "dev is missing the Job/Build permission" when the user can read but not build the downstream job, and Messages.properties (lines 23-30) contains no such message - i.e. the shipped source cannot produce that behavior. This is reported as one lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
